vignette:
At thirty-four, she works the early shift as a prison guard, waking before dawn in the small apartment she shares with her husband. She moves quietly so she does not wake him, though she is rarely sleeping deeply enough to need that kind of care herself. Most nights she drifts off in fragments and then jerks awake, heart pounding, unsure for a few seconds whether she is in her own bedroom or back at the border years ago, holding her younger cousin's hand so tightly that both of them cried.

She left her home country in her twenties, after months of escalating danger that had slowly turned ordinary life into something unrecognizable. At first it was threats spoken indirectly, then men lingering outside the family shop, then a neighbor disappearing. She remembers her mother insisting they stay calm, stay polite, not attract attention. But fear settled into the house anyway. By the time she decided to leave, she no longer walked anywhere without scanning behind her. She slept in her clothes. She kept her documents hidden under a loose floor tile.

The journey north is what returns to her most often now. She does not tell it all at once. Over several conversations, she describes crowded buses, safe houses that were not safe, the smell of sweat and diesel, and the constant need to judge whom to trust in seconds. One night, a group she is traveling with is stopped by armed men. She still speaks of that moment in the present tense, as if it has never fully ended. Everyone freezes. No one knows what will happen. She remembers a child whimpering and a woman praying under her breath. She is sure they might all be taken, assaulted, killed, or simply vanish. Nothing around her feels solid except terror. Even after they are allowed to move on, her body does not seem to understand that the danger has passed. She keeps shaking for hours. From then on, she feels as if she has left part of herself behind on that road.

She eventually makes it to the United States, reunited later with relatives, then building a life that from the outside appears steady. She learns the systems, improves her English, marries a man she describes as patient and hardworking. When she takes the job at the prison, she tells herself she can handle it because she already knows what it means to stay alert. In some ways, the work suits her. She is dependable, observant, hard to rattle in a visible way. Other officers respect that she notices tension before it escalates. She knows which inmate is becoming agitated, which corridor feels off, which voice over the radio carries urgency.

But the same qualities that make her competent at work also trap her in a constant state of readiness. The clang of metal doors can shoot through her like an electric current. If an inmate shouts suddenly, her vision narrows and her palms flood with sweat before she can think. During cell searches she feels the old border fear rising in her throat-her mind flashes to being surrounded, watched, at someone else's mercy. She hates when supervisors stand too close behind her. She tells herself, This is different, you are safe, you are the officer here, but her body does not believe her.

At home, her husband has learned not to touch her unexpectedly when she is cooking or folding laundry. If he comes up behind her, she startles so violently that she sometimes knocks things over. He asks if she is all right, and she says, "I'm just tired," because it feels easier than explaining how often she is elsewhere. She avoids Spanish-language news because reports about migration raids or violence leave her shaky and irritable for the rest of the day. Family members sometimes urge her to be grateful, to focus on how far she has come. She already knows that. The problem is that gratitude does not stop the images.

She tries hard not to think about the journey, but memories intrude anyway: in the shower, during count, while waiting in line at the grocery store. Sometimes it is a full scene; other times just the sound of boots on gravel or the feeling of her cousin's damp hand in hers. She becomes withdrawn when this happens, as though a pane of glass drops between her and everyone else. Her husband says her name twice before she hears him. On her days off, she often plans to go out with friends or visit family, then cancels at the last minute because crowded places feel like too much work. She prefers sitting where she can see the door. She checks locks repeatedly at night, then feels embarrassed by it, then checks again.

What troubles her most is not only fear but the way it has changed her sense of herself. She used to think of herself as warm, social, quick to laugh. Now she often feels flat or distant, especially after difficult shifts. She carries guilt about the relatives who did not make it out and about the version of herself who survived by becoming hard. She knows she is competent. She knows she is loved. Yet much of the time she moves through the world as if danger is still approaching, just not yet visible.
